Valletta, April. In St John's Co-Cathedral, Professor Ruggeri and Giulia are preparing the analyses of the T under Caravaggio's signature. Pietro is attending as an observer. The professor reminds him of the condition: he must ask questions.
So, Pietro. The questions. You promised me.
Why did nobody see the T for four hundred years?
Excellent question. There are two causes. The first is the varnish: over time it turns yellow as an effect of oxidation.
Air, light and candle smoke. It follows that the red turns brown, and the T disappears into the blood.
A restoration in 1956. Someone retouched the signature and, following that retouch, the T was almost completely covered.
Then how did I manage to see it?
Thanks to the cleaning two years ago. And thanks to the fact that you were looking where nobody looks.
And today what are we looking for?
We're trying to understand how it was made. With a brush, with a stick, with a finger. Each tool leaves different traces.
And if we find the answer?
Then we'll have a piece of data. Not proof. Data is compatible with a hypothesis; proof demonstrates it. Remember that.

They left for Malta on 14 April, five of them: Professor Ruggeri, Giulia, Karl, Pietro and a metal case as big as a fridge, which held the instruments for the analyses and which Ruggeri never left, not even for a second, from Rome airport to St John's Co-Cathedral. Karl had come as interpreter and assistant: he spoke Maltese, English and Italian, and knew every corner of Valletta. Pietro had come as an observer, with the permission of his school, his parents, his grandmother and, above all, the professor. On the plane, while the others slept, he opened the black notebook and wrote at the top of a blank page: "Questions for Ruggeri". Below it, the first: "Why did nobody see it before?"

Dr Camilleri was waiting for them at the door of the Co-Cathedral at eight in the evening, when the tourists had already left. He was a small, round man with a white beard and an enormous bunch of keys on his belt, who hugged Giulia like an old friend and shook Ruggeri's hand with the slightly cool courtesy reserved for famous colleagues. Then he looked Pietro up and down and smiled. "So this is the boy of the T," he said in Italian. "Do you know that because of you I received three hundred emails from journalists this year?" Pietro blushed. Camilleri patted him on the shoulder. "Don't worry. I've worked here for forty years and nobody had ever written to me. You've made me famous."

The oratory was dark and silent. Camilleri switched on the lights one at a time, as in a theatre, and the Beheading of St John the Baptist emerged from the darkness, enormous, five metres by three and a half, with the saint's body on the ground, the executioner bending with his knife, the old woman with her hands on her head, the prisoners watching from the window. And at the bottom, in the red of the blood flowing from the Baptist's neck, the signature: "f. MichelAn…", the only signature Caravaggio ever left on a painting. Under the signature, so small that you had to know where to look, was the T. Pietro looked at it the way you look at someone you know in an unexpected place. It had been there for four hundred years. And for four hundred years nobody had seen it. Except him.

The next morning the analyses began. Ruggeri opened the metal case as you open a treasure chest and took out the instruments one at a time, explaining to Pietro what each one was for. The first was an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer, a sort of grey pistol which, held a centimetre from the canvas, told you which chemical elements the paint was made of without touching it. The second was a camera for infrared reflectography, which saw beneath the layers of paint like a gentle X-ray. The third was a digital microscope, connected to a computer, which magnified the surface of the painting two hundred times. "None of these instruments touches the painting," said Ruggeri. "That's the first rule. You look, you measure, you think. You don't touch."

Pietro asked the first question on his list, and Ruggeri answered with a lesson that lasted an hour. There were two causes why the T had remained invisible, he explained. The first was the varnish. Every old painting is covered by a layer of transparent varnish that protects it. But over time, as an effect of oxidation, the varnish turns yellow and darkens. Oxidation is caused by air, light and, in churches, above all by candle smoke. "In four centuries, millions of candles have been lit in this oratory," said Ruggeri. "It follows that the red of the blood has become almost brown. And a small red T inside a brown stain is like an ant in a cup of coffee."

The second cause was more recent, and more embarrassing. In 1956 the painting had been restored in Rome, at the Istituto Centrale, by a restorer who had wanted, as was the custom then, to "tidy up" the signature. With a fine brush he had gone over the faded letters and, following that retouch, the T had been almost completely covered by a stroke of new red. "He didn't do it out of malice," said Ruggeri. "In those days people thought restoring meant making beautiful. Today we think it means making true." The cleaning two years earlier, carried out by Giulia and Matei, had removed the yellowed varnish and the 1956 retouch. Thanks to that cleaning the T had reappeared. And thanks to a boy who looked where nobody looks, someone had noticed it.

The analyses lasted four days. Every evening, when the tourists had gone, Ruggeri, Giulia and Karl worked until midnight, while Pietro took notes and asked questions. Ruggeri, who in Rome was famous for not tolerating interruptions, answered them all. Even the strange ones. On the second day Pietro asked why it was so hot in the oratory, even in the evening. Camilleri, who was passing, stopped. "That," he said, "is the question that keeps me awake at night." And he explained that every day more than two thousand visitors entered the Co-Cathedral. Each one breathed, sweated, brought in the humidity of the street. It followed that the humidity of the air, in summer, reached seventy per cent. And humidity, for a painting on canvas, was enemy number one.

Camilleri took them to his office, a room full of charts pinned to the wall, and showed them the humidity curves of the last ten years. They rose a little more every year. "It's partly due to the visitors," he said, "partly to the climate. Summers in Malta are getting hotter and more humid. The sea is two degrees warmer than when I was a boy." He explained that humidity causes the canvas to expand, swelling at night and shrinking by day, and that this continuous movement, repeated for years, causes small cracks in the paint. "The painting breathes, like us," he said. "But if it breathes too much, it gets ill." For this reason, the following year, the Co-Cathedral would install a new air-conditioning system, which would cost two million euros.

Pietro looked at the charts for a long time, then asked a question that seemed logical to him. "So it's the tourists who are ruining the painting," he said. "Wouldn't it be better to close the church?" Camilleri laughed, but it wasn't a cheerful laugh. "That's the question everyone asks me," he replied. "And the answer is no. Without tourists there would be no tickets, and without tickets there would be no money for restorations. Your restoration two years ago was paid for by them." He explained that the solution was not to close but to regulate: entry at fixed times, smaller groups, a limit on the number of people in the oratory. "The problem isn't the tourist," he concluded, "but the number of tourists at the same time." Pietro smiled. It was almost the same sentence he had said himself, in December, in the final of the tournament. Apparently, he thought, the right ideas work in every language and on every island.

The first result came on the third day, from the spectrometer. Ruggeri placed the grey pistol first on the signature, then on the T, then on the surrounding blood, and compared the three spectra on the computer screen. They were identical. The same red, the same iron, the same mercury from the cinnabar, the same small trace of lead. "The T was made with the same paint as the signature," said Ruggeri slowly. "And with the same paint as the blood." Giulia looked at him. "So it's not a later addition," she said. "It's not an eighteenth-century forger, nor a nineteenth-century restorer." Ruggeri nodded. "It follows that it was made in that workshop, at that moment. With that red. It cannot be ruled out that it was made with the same brush."

It was then that Pietro asked the question that wasn't on the list. He was looking at the microscope screen, where the T appeared magnified two hundred times, like a landscape of red hills. "Professor," he said, "the T doesn't look as if it was made with a brush. The signature has thin lines, you can see the bristles. The T doesn't. It's round. It looks… squashed." Ruggeri came closer to the screen. He remained silent for a long moment. Then he asked Karl to increase the magnification to five hundred times, and to change the angle of the light, raking, almost parallel to the canvas. On the screen, inside the T, very thin lines appeared, curved, concentric, like the ripples a stone makes in water. Giulia held her breath. Karl said something in Maltese that nobody understood. Ruggeri took off his glasses.

"It's a print," he said quietly. "A fingerprint. The T wasn't made with a brush. It was made with a finger. With the fingertip, while the paint was still wet." Nobody spoke. Ruggeri measured the width of the lines with the microscope software, then the distance between one line and the next, then did a calculation on a sheet of paper, in pencil, as he had done as a student. He did it again twice. "The distance between the ridges is about four tenths of a millimetre," he said at last. "In an adult it's five tenths or more. This data is compatible with a child's finger. Six, seven, perhaps eight years old." He paused. "Compatible," he repeated, looking Pietro in the eye. "Not proven. It could also be a woman with very small hands. Remember that."

Pietro remembered. But that night, in the little guesthouse on Strait Street where they were staying, he couldn't sleep a wink. He was thinking about the register of the knights' hospital, from September 1608: "Agata, Sicilian laundress, with her son Salvatore, aged seven". He was thinking about the child hidden under the black of the Saint Lucy in Syracuse, the one he himself had named Totò. He was thinking about a seven-year-old child in the workshop of a wanted painter, dipping a finger into the red of the blood, still wet, and writing the first letter of his name under the master's. Totò. Salvatore. T. Everything was compatible. Nothing was proven. At three in the morning he switched on the light and wrote in the notebook, under the questions: "Compatible doesn't mean true. But it doesn't mean false either."

The next day was Sunday, and the Co-Cathedral was closed for Mass. Karl took everyone to lunch at his mother's, in Marsaxlokk, the fishing village in the south of the island, where the colourful boats have an eye painted on the prow to protect them from the evil eye. Mrs Borg was a tiny woman, dressed in black, who didn't speak Italian but understood everything, and who had been cooking for three days. She greeted Ruggeri by calling him "Gentile professore", in Italian learned specially for the occasion, and everyone burst out laughing, except Ruggeri, who didn't know the story of the letters and was very flattered. During lunch Karl translated his mother's questions: whether Pietro ate enough, whether Giulia had children, whether the professor was married. Ruggeri said no. Mrs Borg said something in Maltese, and Karl refused to translate it.

Before dessert, Mrs Borg stood up, went to her bedroom and came back with an envelope in her hand. It was the letter Karl had written to her in February, by hand, in Maltese, with the last line in Italian. She showed it to everyone proudly, pointing at the final sentence: "I look forward to hearing from you." Then, through Karl, she explained that she had asked the village priest to translate it for her, and that the priest had laughed for five minutes. So she had decided to reply in Italian too, with the priest's help, and had begun with "Gentile figlio". Karl covered his face with his hands. Ruggeri, who had finally understood the story, laughed until he cried. At the end of lunch Mrs Borg gave Pietro a small painted wooden eye, like the ones on the boats. "To see what others don't see," Karl translated. Pietro put it in the black notebook, next to the page of questions.

After lunch, while the others drank coffee on the terrace overlooking the harbour, Ruggeri and Pietro walked down together to the quay. The professor walked slowly, hands in his pockets, looking at the boats. For a while he said nothing. Then he stopped. "You know, Pietro," he said, "in thirty years I've seen dozens of wonderful hypotheses. Secret children, hidden lovers, coded messages. Almost all of them were false. And the people who had made them didn't want to admit it, because they had fallen in love with their hypothesis. It's the most dangerous disease for a scholar." Pietro listened, looking at the water. "And this one?" he asked. Ruggeri thought for a long time. "This one is different," he said. "Because you, so far, have never said it's true. You've only asked questions. And every question has led us to a piece of data."

On the last day, before closing the metal case, Ruggeri wrote the report for the Co-Cathedral and read it aloud to everyone, in Camilleri's office. It was written in the most cautious language Pietro had ever heard. "The non-invasive analyses carried out on the letter T have revealed the following. First: the pigment is identical to that of the signature; it follows that the letter is contemporary with the work. Second: the letter was not executed with a brush, but with the tip of a finger, while the paint was wet. Third: the dimensions of the print are compatible with those of a child aged between six and eight. It cannot be ruled out that it is an adult with small hands. The identity of the author remains unknown."

Camilleri asked whether something more couldn't be written. The journalists, he said, would want a name. Ruggeri shook his head. "The journalists will write what they like," he said. "We write what we know." Then, however, he added a line by hand, at the bottom of the report, before his signature. He read it in a low voice: "Thanks are due to the young observer Pietro, without whose questions, including those not strictly necessary, this research would not have been possible." Pietro blushed to the roots of his hair. Giulia squeezed his arm. Karl applauded on his own, then stopped, embarrassed. Camilleri took out of a drawer a bottle of prickly pear liqueur and four little glasses, plus a glass of orange juice for Pietro, and they drank a toast to the T.

On the flight home Ruggeri sat next to Pietro and, for the first time since they had met, talked about himself. He told him that he too, at fourteen, had made a discovery. He was in Rome, in the church of San Luigi dei Francesi, in front of the Calling of St Matthew, and had noticed that Christ's hand was the same as the hand of Michelangelo's Adam, reversed. He had told his art history teacher, who had laughed in his face. "Then I found out everyone knew," said Ruggeri, smiling. "It wasn't a discovery. But that laugh made me want to become what I am. So that I would never laugh in the face of a boy asking a question." He looked out of the window, towards the sea. "I came close to doing it, with you. On television. I apologise."

Pietro didn't know what to answer. So he did the only thing that came into his head: he opened the black notebook at the page of questions and handed it to him. Ruggeri read it all, from beginning to end: forty-seven questions, some serious, some funny, some that didn't yet have an answer. The last one, written that morning at the airport, said: "If one day it were discovered that the T really is Totò's, what would change?" Ruggeri looked at it for a long time. Then he took Pietro's pen and wrote the answer underneath, in his small professor's handwriting. "For the painting, nothing. For art history, a footnote. For a seven-year-old child who in 1608 put his finger in the master's paint, everything. That's why it's worth continuing to search."

In Florence, at the trattoria, everyone was waiting for them. Graziella had made ribollita, Davide had drawn an enormous red finger on a placard saying "Welcome back, detectives", Viola ran between the tables shouting "the T! the T!" without really knowing what it was. Bellini, sitting at his table, listened to Giulia's account from beginning to end, without interrupting, his hands clasped on his stick. When she got to the fingerprint, he closed his eyes. Then he asked Pietro to show him the page of the notebook with Ruggeri's answer. He read it twice. "Ernesto used to say that every painting has inside it the hands of the person who made it," he said at last. "I didn't think he meant it literally." Then he smiled. "For four hundred years that child waited for someone his own age to see him. Adults look at signatures. Children look at fingerprints."
